\chapter{Writing --- My Own Line}
\label{ch:ar-satri-al-khass}
\hlchaptermodality{43}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write one line of Arabic about myself from a closed supply of known words, choosing not only the words but the shape each letter takes where it stands.}

Complete AR-W02-satri-al-khass: one line chosen rather than copied, with the joins checked before anything else.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[(my own line)]{My own line — the first writing with no model}

\label{lesson:AR-W02-satri-al-khass}



\begin{quote}
Everything you have written so far had something to reach for.

This does not. You choose the words, from a supply that is closed: only what this book has taught you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — controlled composition}
Write \textbf{one line} about yourself, right to left.

And here is the extra decision Arabic asks for that most scripts do not. A letter does not have one shape. It has up to \textbf{four}, and which one you write depends on \textbf{where in the word it stands} — alone, at the start, in the middle, at the end.

Copying hid that from you: the model already showed the right shape. Choosing your own words means choosing the shapes too, and a letter you have only ever copied in the middle of a word is a letter you may not yet be able to start one with.

Write the line. Then read it back and check the \textbf{joins} before you check anything else — a letter that should have connected and did not is the error a reader notices first.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many shapes can one Arabic letter have? (\textbf{Up to four.})

And what decides which one you write? (\textbf{Where it stands in the word.})
\end{tcolorbox}
